title: The good friend who chooses
hook: the friend who closes your menu and orders for you; should a teacher choose your practice, or should you test it yourself?
tomorrow: a house, family, even books. what could they get in the way of?

segments.voice: Yesterday: suited to you, six temperaments read from a broom and a breakfast. But who does the reading? That's where the argument starts.

At a new restaurant, there's always that one friend who closes your menu and says: trust me, i'll order. Some people love that friend. Some would rather go hungry. Buddhaghosa's answer to who should choose your meditation subject sounds like the menu friend: traditionally, the teacher does. And inside the tradition, that answer has a strong rival.
screen: `TRUST ME, I'LL ORDER.` → `THE TEACHER CHOOSES.` → `AND A STRONG RIVAL.`

segments.voice: View one: the Visuddhimagga. Go to a good friend, a kalyanamitta, someone who knows the path, who can watch how you live and then give you the subject that fits. Temperament is hard to read from the inside; the one holding the broom rarely sees the dust. Behind this sits an exchange from the suttas. Ananda says good friendship is half of the holy life, and the Buddha answers: not so. It's the whole of it. View two: the Kalama Sutta. The Kalamas tell the Buddha they're confused, since every teacher who passes through praises his own way. He tells them: don't go by reports, or tradition, or scripture, or clever reasoning, or because this teacher is ours. When you know for yourselves that something leads to harm, drop it. When you know it leads to good, take it up. Now, each side's best case. The Kalama side protects you from a teacher who's wrong, or worse; it keeps your own eyes open. The good-friend side protects you from your blind spots; nobody sees the back of their own head. And they may not cancel each other out. In Buddhaghosa's picture, the friend chooses, and you still find out in your own practice whether it helps. A friend chooses. You do the walking.
screen: `VIEW ONE: THE GOOD FRIEND CHOOSES.` · `NOT HALF THE HOLY LIFE: ALL OF IT.` · `VIEW TWO: KNOW FOR YOURSELVES.` · `BLIND SPOTS VS. A WRONG TEACHER.` · then, large: `A FRIEND CHOOSES.`

segments.voice: Think of one person who has seen you at your best and at your worst. Write them a short question that only someone who knows you could answer, like: what am i good at that i can't see? Send it, or keep it as a draft until it feels right.
The good friend who chooses: in the Visuddhimagga, the kalyanamitta, the teacher who reads you and gives the meditation subject.

segments.voice: Something to keep: a friend chooses, and you still do the walking. Three of forty, done.

howItsDone: In Theravada monasteries and meditation centers, a student may receive a meditation subject from a teacher and report back on how it goes; lay meditators can check their practice with a teacher too.

fork.setup: your friend says: "nobody should choose your path for you. the Buddha said test everything yourself." what's the best case for letting a teacher choose?
options: a good friend sees your blind spots, and you still test what they give.
teachers have authority, so questioning them is disrespectful.
the Kalama Sutta doesn't really count; it's a minor teaching.
fork.reveal: both views stand in the tradition. the good friend covers what you can't see in yourself; the Kalama Sutta keeps your own eyes open. a friend chooses; you do the walking.

original.note: Pali: good friend, admirable friend; in meditation, the teacher who gives the subject.

trapdoor: what you thought: a good friend is someone fun to hang out with.
what it means: in the Visuddhimagga, the good friend is the teacher who watches how you live and gives the meditation subject that fits.
what a scholar hears: the Upaddha Sutta (SN 45.2) calls good friendship the whole of the holy life, while the Kalama Sutta (AN 3.65) warns against going by a teacher's word alone.
guess: a trusted teacher who reads you and picks your practice
a classmate who meditates beside you for motivation
a guardian spirit believed to watch over meditators

chat.says: ms. reyes offered to just pick my theme. ava says i'd be giving up my voice. who's right?
options: Let her suggest; she sees your blind spots. Then test it in your own work.
Ava's right. Only you can know what suits you, so choose alone.
Let her pick and stop thinking. The teacher always knows best.
chat.meaning: Buddhaghosa's good friend chooses because you can't fully read yourself; the Kalama Sutta adds: know for yourself whether it helps. Both together.

kalyanamitta.meaning: Pali: good friend; a teacher who gives the meditation subject

Ananda.meaning: the Buddha's cousin and close attendant

Kalama Sutta.meaning: a discourse telling the Kalamas to know for themselves

Visuddhimagga.meaning: 'The Path of Purification,' Buddhaghosa's guide to the path

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga III.28, III.57–65 (approach the good friend, the giver of the meditation subject)
Samyutta Nikaya 45.2, Upaddha Sutta (good friendship is the whole of the holy life)
Anguttara Nikaya 3.65, Kalama Sutta (do not go by reports, tradition, scripture, reasoning, or 'this teacher is ours'; know for yourselves)

notes: All three sources paraphrased; confirm Visuddhimagga section numbers for the good friend as giver of the subject, and the list of 'don't go by' items in the Kalama Sutta (shortened in the voice).

Debate shape: Visuddhimagga's teacher-chooses vs the Kalama Sutta's 'know for yourselves'; the lesson lets both speak and suggests they may not cancel (the student still tests the subject in practice). Confirm this is fair to both.
